text: All right, DJ, thanks for coming on Houston. We have a podcast today. Thanks for having me. We're happy to have you and we're excited to talk about Ellington operations today. Yeah, absolutely. So I'm retired from the Air Force. Retired in 2009. I was a pilot there. And as far as how I kind of initially got into flying, my father was a pilot in the Air Force, so I was kind of always around airplanes. So anyway, went through college, graduated from RPI with an engineering degree, and then went into the Air Force as a pilot. It was established all the way back in World War I to become a training base for pilots that were going to go over, you know, to the war. It ended up at times closing down for small periods, but then it was re-established during World War II, and once again became a big training base for the Army Air Forces then. Nowadays, I think every single service with the exception of Space Force is represented at Ellington Field, in addition to NASA. And it, in 2015, became a spaceport. In terms of NASA operations, it really is the same initially as when it was established back with the Mercury 7 astronauts, where we house our T-38s to be used for our astronaut training. So when we're not flying that aircraft, we house it out at El Paso, where we have a forward operating location. And have you done some work out at that facility as well? Yeah, we tend to fly out there a fair amount. And we did a lot of operations out at the FOL in El Paso, especially during the shuttle era. Our shuttle training aircraft would go out there to practice up on the White Sands Missile Range. So we've talked about this a little bit, but can you name all of the different aircraft that are currently based out at Ellington? Yeah so again the T we possess 20 T that are used for what we call spaceflight readiness training We possess three WB that are used for high research We have one Gulfstream V aircraft that is used for our astronaut direct return missions, in addition to other scientific research. And then our Super Guppy aircraft that, like I said, is out at El Paso. So are there any particularly rare or specialized aircraft? I think of the Guppy when I think of something like that, but is that what you would consider specialized? Yeah, absolutely. The Guppy is one of one. It is the only one flying in the world. So, and it's there for us to be able to carry outside space hardware. It's cross-sectional area is actually the biggest of any aircraft in the world. So, it can't carry as big a payload as say a military C-5 or C-17, but it can carry very, very outsized things like cross sections of rocket engines or space capsules, etc. In addition, our WB-57s are highly specialized. Those are the only three of those flying in the world. Yeah. So we get to do some neat things. Can you try to put into perspective how big the Guppy is? Do you have the measurements for it or can you compare it to something similar in size? the the guppy is actually based on what was a kc-97 tanker which was essentially and there was a version of that that was actually an airliner at the time so if you think kind of boeing 707 although that's a jet it's about that size only the fuselage has been uh enlarged significantly hence the guppy name so do you have to have some sort of specialized pilot's license to pilot an aircraft like that? You don't have to have a specialized pilot's license for that in particular. In fact, it's kind of interesting, like say to fly the T-38 or to fly an aircraft like the Guppy, you actually don't have to have a pilot's license. We are able to fly that under what we call public use. However, you have to have some very special skills in order to fly that aircraft. And that is, I do not personally fly that one, but it is easily probably the most difficult aircraft in our fleet to fly. I would assume so. That is so cool. And I also did not realize that that was the only one in the world. Only one. How cool. Right here in Houston, Texas at Ellington Field sometime.
